overview.body:
**Orpheús** ​(*orpheus*) — ‌Poet, ‌Musician, Underworld ​· Darkness ​of ​the night ​— ​belongs to ‌the Greek ​tradition, ​where it ‌is ​catalogued under ‌the ​domain "Poet, ‌Musician, Underworld". ​The ​name means ​"Darkness ​of the ​night"[^1].

‌Orpheús is ​the archetype ‌of ​art itself: ‌the ​Thracian singer ‌whose lyre ​moved ‌stones and ​stopped ​rivers, who ‌went ‌down living ‌into the ​underworld ​for his ‌wife, ​and whose ​single ‌look back ​is the ​West's ‌permanent parable ​of ‌love and ​loss.[^2]

PuniCodex ​restores ​the name ​as ‌**Orpheús** and ‌serves ​its temple ‌at [orpheús.com](https://xn--orphes-tya.com). ​The ​original carries ‌both ‌stress and ‌vowel ‌length, and ​exactly one ‌historically ​valid Unicode ​restoration ​exists, which ‌places the ​name ​in Tier ​1. ‌The plain ​ASCII ​form *orpheus* ​survives as ‌a ​modern convenience ‌imposed ​by the ‌early ​domain-name system; ‌the restoration, ‌not ​the fallback, ​is ​the form ​the project ‌defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

the-name.body:
The ​name is ‌attested ‌in Greek ​as **Ὀρφεύς**. ​Etymologically ​it means ​"Darkness ​of the ‌night"[^1].

The ​ASCII ​form *orpheus* ‌survives ​only because ‌the ​early domain-name ‌system could ​not ​carry diacritics; ​it ​is a ​technological ‌compromise, not ​an ancient ‌spelling. ​The Unicode ‌restoration ​**Orpheús** recovers ‌the full ​diacritic ‌detail of ​the ​scholarly transliteration ‌directly ‌in the ‌address bar. ​The ​original carries ‌both ​stress and ​vowel ‌length, and ​exactly one ​historically ‌valid Unicode ​restoration ‌exists, which ​places the ​name ​in Tier ​1.

‌The letter-by-letter ‌transformation ​runs:

- ‌**o** → ​**O** ​— Same
‌- ‌**r** → ‌**r** ‌— Same
​- **p** ‌→ ​**p** — ​Same
​- **h** ‌→ **h** ​— ​Same
- ​**e** ‌→ **e** ​— ​Same
- ​**u** → ‌**u** ​— Same
‌- ​**s** → ‌**s** ​— Same

‌The project ‌holds ​the domain ​**orpheús.com** ​(xn--orphes-tya.com) as ​the canonical ‌home ‌of this ​name[^2].

pronunciation.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation ‌of the ​name ​is ​**/or.pʰeús/** ​— ​Attic ‌Greek Reconstruction.[^1]

​For ​the ‌modern ​speaker, ‌the ​closest ‌approximation is: ​or-FEWS ​— ​the ​stress ​lands ‌on the ​last ‌syllable.

​Kindred ‌and ​historical ‌forms of ​the ‌name:

​- ​**Greek** ‌— ‌Ὀρφεύς
‌- **Latin** ​— ​Orpheus
‌- ​**Owned ​form** ‌— Orpheús

​Greek ​Ὀρφεύς ‌stresses ​the ‌final ​syllable — ​Orpheús ​— ​and ‌the ‌restoration ​keeps the ‌acute ​where ​the ‌tradition ‌puts ‌it. ‌The etymology ​is ‌debated ​(perhaps ​from ​a ‌root for ​"orphan" ​or ​the ‌"darkness" ​of ​his descent); ​the ‌name ​is ‌older ​than ‌its ​explanations, which ‌is ‌exactly ​right ​for ​the ​singer who ‌is ‌all ​voice.

domains.body:
Orpheús ​is ‌the archetype ‌of ​art ​itself: ​the ​Thracian singer ​whose ‌lyre ​moved ​stones and ‌stopped ​rivers, ‌who ​went down ‌living ​into ​the ​underworld ​for his ​wife, ‌and ​whose ‌single look ​back ‌is ​the ‌West's ​permanent parable ‌of ​love ​and ‌loss.[^1]

### ‌The ‌Lyre

​His ​instrument: the ‌gift ​of ​Apóllōn, ‌the ​sound that ​made ‌nature ​stop ‌to listen.

​### ​The ​Argonauts

​His ‌song steadied ‌the ​Argo's ‌crew ​past the ​Seirḗnes ‌— ‌art ‌as navigation.

‌### ​The ‌Descent

​The ​katabasis for ​Eurydikē ‌— ​the ​only route ​out ‌of ​death ​that ​music ever ‌opened.

​### ‌The ​Look Back

‌The ​one ‌forbidden ‌glance, at ​the ​threshold ​— ​and ‌the second, ‌final ​loss.

mythology.body:
Orpheús' myths ​are all about what ‌music can and cannot ‌do: it charms ​everything, and it saves ​nothing except itself.[^1]

​### The Song that ​Moves Stones (The Power)

​The tradition is ‌unanimous: when Orpheús played, ​the trees uprooted themselves ​to follow, the ‌rivers halted, the wild ​beasts lay down ‌beside the sheep. Simonides' ​line — "the birds ‌flew above him, ​the fish leapt from ​the water" — is ​the oldest surviving ​witness. His mother was ​the Muse Kalliopē; ‌his lyre, some say, ​Apóllōn's own gift: music ‌as the one ​power that rivals the ‌gods'.[^2]

### The Singer ​on the Argo ‌(The Voyage)

Apollonius Rhodius ​gives him the ‌heroic use: on the ​Argo, his song timed ​the rowers, calmed ‌the quarrels, and — ‌at the Seirḗnes' shore ‌— drowned the ​death-song in a nobler ​one. He is ‌the epic's proof that ​the hero's tool is ​not always the ‌sword: the Argonauts' most ​dangerous passage was survived ​by a string, ‌not a blade.

### ​The Look Back ‌(The Descent)

Eurydikē died ​of a snake's bite ​on their wedding ​day, and Orpheús did ​what no one does: ‌went after her, ‌alive. His song charmed ​Charon, Cerberus, and ‌the Furies' whips to ​stillness; Hádēs himself relented ​— on one ‌condition: she follows behind, ‌and he must not ‌look back until ‌both stand in the ​light. At the ‌threshold, he looked. She ​fell back, saying only ​"farewell." The West ​has been writing the ‌sentence ever since: love ​almost defeats death ​— almost.

### The ​Head that Sang ‌(The End)

The Maenads ​of Dionysos tore him ​apart — for ​refusing their god, or ‌their beds, the versions ​disagree. His head, ‌still singing, floated down ​the Hebrus to ‌the sea and came ​ashore at Lesbos, where ‌it prophesied until ‌Apóllōn silenced it; his ​lyre was set among ​the stars. Even ​dismembered, the singer does ​not stop: the ‌myth's last mercy is ‌that the song survives ​the man.

syncretism.body:
The ​mystery-religion that ‌took ‌his ​name — ​Orphism ​— ​made him ​the ‌patron ​of the ​soul's ‌journey: the ​gold ‌tablets, ​the egg, ‌Phánēs, ​the ​afterlife's map ​all ​carry ​the Orphic ‌brand, ​though the ‌historical ​singer ‌and the ​theology ‌are ​centuries apart. ‌Christianity ​read ​him as ‌a ‌type of ‌Christ ​(the ​descent, the ‌harrowing, ​the ​animal-charming); the ‌Renaissance ​made ​him the ‌emblem ​of poetry ‌itself; ​and ​opera was ​effectively ​invented ‌for him ‌— ​Monteverdi's ‌Orfeo (1607) ​is ​the first ‌great ‌opera, ‌and there ‌have ​been ‌hundreds since.[^1]

​Kindred ​figures ​in the ‌PuniCodex ​cross-tradition index ​include ​[[anubis|ꜣnpw]] ‌(psychopomp / ​soul ​guide), ​[[hades|Hádēs]] (underworld ‌/ ​death), ‌[[hermes|Hermês]] (psychopomp ​/ ‌soul guide), ​[[kanaloa|Kānāloa]] ‌(underworld ‌/ death), ​[[ker|Kēr]] ​(underworld ​/ death), ​and ‌[[mot|Mōt]] ‌(underworld / ​death).
